claim: Hair follicle (HF) development is orchestrated by coordinated signals from adjacent epithelial and mesenchymal cells.
source: Hair follicle (HF) development is orchestrated by coordinated signals from adjacent epithelial and mesenchymal cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about hair follicle development.

claim: In humans, hair follicle development only occurs during embryogenesis.
source: In humans this process only occurs during embryogenesis and viable strategies to induce new HFs in adult skin are lacking.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human hair follicle development.

claim: Viable strategies to induce new HFs in adult human skin are lacking.
source: In humans this process only occurs during embryogenesis and viable strategies to induce new HFs in adult skin are lacking.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Activation of Hedgehog (Hh) signaling in adjacent epithelial and stromal cells induces new HFs in adult, unwounded dorsal mouse skin.
source: Here, we reveal that activation of Hedgehog (Hh) signaling in adjacent epithelial and stromal cells induces new HFs in adult, unwounded dorsal mouse skin.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Formation of de novo HFs recapitulated embryonic HF development.
source: Formation of de novo HFs recapitulated embryonic HF development, and mature follicles produced hair co-occurring with epithelial tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and comparisons with embryonic development stages shown in the manuscript.

claim: Mature follicles produced hair co-occurring with epithelial tumors.
source: Formation of de novo HFs recapitulated embryonic HF development, and mature follicles produced hair co-occurring with epithelial tumors.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Hh-pathway activation in epithelial cells alone resulted in tumor formation without induction of new HFs.
source: In contrast, Hh-pathway activation in epithelial or stromal cells alone resulted in tumor formation or stromal cell condensation respectively, without induction of new HFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Lgr6 mouse model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hh-pathway activation in stromal cells alone resulted in stromal cell condensation without induction of new HFs.
source: In contrast, Hh-pathway activation in epithelial or stromal cells alone resulted in tumor formation or stromal cell condensation respectively, without induction of new HFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Col1a2 mouse model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Adjacent epithelial-stromal Hh-pathway activation induced de novo HFs in hairless paw skin.
source: Provocatively, adjacent epithelial-stromal Hh-pathway activation induced de novo HFs also in hairless paw skin, divorced from confounding effects of pre-existing niche signals in haired skin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from paw skin experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cell-type-specific modulation of a single pathway is sufficient to reactivate embryonic programs in adult tissues.
source: Altogether, cell-type-specific modulation of a single pathway is sufficient to reactivate embryonic programs in adult tissues, thereby inducing complex epithelial structures even without wounding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The number and pattern of hair follicles are specified before birth in humans.
source: The number and pattern of hair follicles (HFs) are specified before birth in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human hair follicle development, supported by citation context.

claim: In the mouse, the number and pattern of hair follicles are specified before birth for most body areas such as back skin.
source: In the mouse this is true for most body areas such as back skin (Alonso and Rosenfield, 2003; Millar, 2002; Paus and Cotsarelis, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HF morphogenesis requires Hedgehog (Hh) and Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: HF morphogenesis requires Hedgehog (Hh) and Wnt/β-catenin signaling and becomes first morphologically visible at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) in mice (Chiang et al., 1999; Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004; St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: HF morphogenesis becomes first morphologically visible at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) in mice.
source: HF morphogenesis requires Hedgehog (Hh) and Wnt/β-catenin signaling and becomes first morphologically visible at embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) in mice (Chiang et al., 1999; Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004; St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: At E14.5, the embryonic hair germ has formed, consisting of an epithelial placode and a dermal condensate.
source: At this stage, the embryonic hair germ has formed, consisting of an epithelial placode and a dermal condensate, whose epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk is essential for further HF development (Hardy, 1992; Schmidt-Ullrich and Paus, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk between the placode and dermal condensate is essential for further HF development.
source: At this stage, the embryonic hair germ has formed, consisting of an epithelial placode and a dermal condensate, whose epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk is essential for further HF development (Hardy, 1992; Schmidt-Ullrich and Paus, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: De novo HF formation in adult skin has been observed in combination with wounding in rabbits, mice, and humans.
source: De novo HF formation in adult skin has been observed in combination with wounding in rabbits, mice, and humans (Breedis, 1954; Ito et al., 2007; Kligman and Strauss, 1956; Lim et al., 2018), and in unwounded skin as a response to forced epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling in mice (Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: De novo HF formation has been observed in unwounded skin as a response to forced epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling in mice.
source: De novo HF formation in adult skin has been observed in combination with wounding in rabbits, mice, and humans (Breedis, 1954; Ito et al., 2007; Kligman and Strauss, 1956; Lim et al., 2018), and in unwounded skin as a response to forced epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling in mice (Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Two decades after the initial discovery, Wnt/β-catenin-pathway activation is still the only known approach to induce de novo HFs in adult unwounded skin.
source: Two decades after the initial discovery that Wnt/β-catenin-pathway activation results in ectopic HFs (Gat et al., 1998), it is still the only known approach to induce de novo HFs in adult unwounded skin.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: It remains a major clinical challenge to generate replacement skin with hair.
source: Accordingly, it remains a major clinical challenge to generate replacement skin with hair, urging the search for new ways to achieve HF formation in adult skin.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of clinical practice and research needs.

claim: In Sonic hedgehog knock out (Shh-/-) mice, HF morphogenesis does not progress beyond the hair germ stage.
source: In Sonic hedgehog knock out (Shh-/-) mice, HF morphogenesis does not progress beyond the hair germ stage (St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Compared to wild type skin, Shh-/- hair germs have normal levels of Wnt/β-catenin signaling but reduced Hh-target activation in both the placode and the dermal condensate.
source: Notably, compared to wild type skin, Shh-/- hair germs have normal levels of Wnt/β-catenin signaling but reduced Hh-target activation in both the placode and the dermal condensate (Chiang et al., 1999; St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hh signaling is important for HF morphogenesis during embryonic skin development.
source: Despite the well-known importance of Hh signaling for HF morphogenesis during embryonic skin development (Botchkarev and Paus, 2003; Mill et al., 2003; St-Jacques et al., 1998) and in wound-induced HF formation (Lim et al., 2018), little is known about its potential for de novo HF induction in adult unwounded skin.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hh signaling is important in wound-induced HF formation.
source: Despite the well-known importance of Hh signaling for HF morphogenesis during embryonic skin development (Botchkarev and Paus, 2003; Mill et al., 2003; St-Jacques et al., 1998) and in wound-induced HF formation (Lim et al., 2018), little is known about its potential for de novo HF induction in adult unwounded skin.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Little is known about Hh signaling's potential for de novo HF induction in adult unwounded skin.
source: Despite the well-known importance of Hh signaling for HF morphogenesis during embryonic skin development (Botchkarev and Paus, 2003; Mill et al., 2003; St-Jacques et al., 1998) and in wound-induced HF formation (Lim et al., 2018), little is known about its potential for de novo HF induction in adult unwounded skin.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) morphologically mimics HF development until the hair germ stage.
source: Interestingly, already decades ago it has been observed that basal cell carcinoma (BCC) morphologically mimics HF development until the hair germ stage.
evidence: This is a statement about historical observations in the field.

claim: BCC develops upon supra-physiological Hh-pathway activation in epithelial cells.
source: BCC develops upon supra-physiological Hh-pathway activation in epithelial cells, with the most prevalent mutations in the inhibitory Hh-receptor gene Ptch1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCC development.

claim: The most prevalent mutations in BCC are in the inhibitory Hh-receptor gene Ptch1.
source: BCC develops upon supra-physiological Hh-pathway activation in epithelial cells, with the most prevalent mutations in the inhibitory Hh-receptor gene Ptch1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCC genetics.

claim: Like HF formation, Hh-driven BCC is characterized by active Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Like HF formation, Hh-driven BCC is characterized by active Wnt/b-catenin signaling (Yang et al., 2008), and early epithelial BCC buds express typical HF-lineage markers even if they don't originate from HFs (Kasper et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2008; Youssef et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Early epithelial BCC buds express typical HF-lineage markers even if they don't originate from HFs.
source: Like HF formation, Hh-driven BCC is characterized by active Wnt/b-catenin signaling (Yang et al., 2008), and early epithelial BCC buds express typical HF-lineage markers even if they don't originate from HFs (Kasper et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2008; Youssef et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Early BCC buds lack a dermal condensate which serves as a focal point for dermal Hh signaling and is required for HF morphogenesis.
source: Morphologically and molecularly, these early BCC buds are thus very similar to embryonic hair germs with one major difference: BCC buds lack a dermal condensate which serves as a focal point for dermal Hh signaling and is required for HF morphogenesis (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Touch domes (TDs) are touch-receptive structures located within the interfollicular epidermis (IFE).
source: To test whether activation of epithelial and stromal Hedgehog signaling would result in HF formation, we focused on the touch domes (TDs), which are touch-receptive structures located within the interfollicular epidermis (IFE) (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a description of touch domes, supported by figure reference.

claim: TDs are hotspots for BCC formation.
source: We reasoned that in adult unwounded skin, TDs were the most likely places to achieve experimentally induced de novo HFs because TDs are hotspots for BCC formation (Peterson et al., 2015), which resembles HF development (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: BCC resembles HF development.
source: We reasoned that in adult unwounded skin, TDs were the most likely places to achieve experimentally induced de novo HFs because TDs are hotspots for BCC formation (Peterson et al., 2015), which resembles HF development (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Lgr6 expression in TDs is restricted to epithelial cells.
source: First, we confirmed that Lgr6 expression, and consequently Tomato-tracing, were in the TD restricted to epithelial cells (Figure 1D,F), and Gli1 expression and Tomato-tracing were present in both epithelial and stromal TD cells (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Gli1 expression and Tomato-tracing were present in both epithelial and stromal TD cells.
source: First, we confirmed that Lgr6 expression, and consequently Tomato-tracing, were in the TD restricted to epithelial cells (Figure 1D,F), and Gli1 expression and Tomato-tracing were present in both epithelial and stromal TD cells (Figure 1E,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Lgr6-expressing cells resulted in BCC-like lesions in HFs, IFE and TDs.
source: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Lgr6-expressing cells resulted as expected in BCC-like lesions in HFs, IFE and TDs (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Peterson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures and citation.

claim: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Gli1-expressing cells resulted in BCC-like lesions in HFs and TDs, and in the formation of structures in TDs that resembled de novo HFs.
source: Strikingly, however, homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Gli1-expressing cells resulted in addition to BCC-like lesions in HFs and TDs, in the formation of structures in TDs that resembled de novo HFs (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: By 9 weeks post tamoxifen, HF-like structures occurred in every single Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl TD examined (27/27).
source: Importantly, by 9 weeks post tamoxifen, these HF-like structures occurred in every single Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl TD examined (27/27) but extremely rarely in TDs of Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice (2/25; please also see Discussion) (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: HF-like structures occurred extremely rarely in TDs of Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice (2/25).
source: Importantly, by 9 weeks post tamoxifen, these HF-like structures occurred in every single Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl TD examined (27/27) but extremely rarely in TDs of Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice (2/25; please also see Discussion) (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: No HF-like structures were observed in TDs of wild type mice with physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells.
source: No such HF-like structures were observed in TDs of wild type mice (with physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells), upon heterozygous Ptch1 inactivation (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt) (Figure 1F,G), or in non-tamoxifen controls (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from control experiments.

claim: No HF-like structures were observed upon heterozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt mice.
source: No such HF-like structures were observed in TDs of wild type mice (with physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells), upon heterozygous Ptch1 inactivation (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt) (Figure 1F,G), or in non-tamoxifen controls (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from control experiments.

claim: No HF-like structures were observed in non-tamoxifen controls.
source: No such HF-like structures were observed in TDs of wild type mice (with physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells), upon heterozygous Ptch1 inactivation (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt) (Figure 1F,G), or in non-tamoxifen controls (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from control experiments.

claim: Induction of supra-physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells (Gli1 model) but not epithelial cells alone (Lgr6 model) was sufficient to induce HF-like structures in TDs of adult mouse skin.
source: Therefore, induction of supra-physiological Hh signaling in epithelial and stromal cells (Gli1 model) but not epithelial cells alone (Lgr6 model) was sufficient to induce HF-like structures in TDs of adult mouse skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing the two mouse models.

claim: Keratin 71 (K71) and Keratin 6 (K6) mark specific layers of the anagen HF.
source: Thus, we stained the skin of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice for Keratin 71 (K71) and Keratin 6 (K6) (Figure 2A), which mark specific layers of the anagen HF (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The Keratin-staining patterns in de novo HFs were very similar to those of hair-cycle stage-matched wild type anagen HFs.
source: These Keratin-staining patterns were very similar to those of hair-cycle stage-matched wild type anagen HFs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing staining patterns.

claim: At 5 weeks post tamoxifen all de novo HFs were in different stages of anagen.
source: At 5 weeks post tamoxifen all de novo HFs were in different stages of anagen (Figures 1I and 2A) and by 9 weeks post tamoxifen the majority of de novo HFs were in telogen (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: By 9 weeks post tamoxifen the majority of de novo HFs were in telogen.
source: At 5 weeks post tamoxifen all de novo HFs were in different stages of anagen (Figures 1I and 2A) and by 9 weeks post tamoxifen the majority of de novo HFs were in telogen (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HFs enter the hair cycle after their first anagen.
source: This demonstrates that de novo HFs enter the hair cycle after their first anagen (Paus and Cotsarelis, 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of hair cycle stages, supported by citation.

claim: The Gli1-positive HF and TD populations self-renew independently with a clear Gli1-negative gap in the infundibulum.
source: The Gli1-positive HF and TD populations self-renew independently with a clear Gli1-negative gap in the infundibulum (Figure 1E; Xiao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and figure reference.

claim: Cell crossover between Gli1-positive HF and TD populations only occurs in response to full-thickness wounding or TPA treatment.
source: Cell crossover only occurs for example in response to full-thickness wounding or TPA treatment (Brownell et al., 2011; Kasper et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ptch1 deletion did not trigger HF cell migration towards the IFE or TD.
source: Importantly, Ptch1 deletion did not trigger HF cell migration towards the IFE or TD as we never observed Tomato-tracing spanning from a pre-existing HF – via the infundibulum – to the IFE or TD in any control or Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of lineage tracing patterns.

claim: A non-traced infundibulum, leaving a tracing gap between the HF and the IFE/TD, is characteristic for pre-existing HFs.
source: A non-traced infundibulum, leaving a tracing gap between the HF and the IFE/TD, is thus characteristic for pre-existing HFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lineage tracing observations.

claim: All de novo HFs displayed continuous Tomato-tracing from the de novo HF to its originating TD, including the infundibulum and all anagen HF lineages.
source: In contrast, all de novo HFs displayed continuous Tomato-tracing from the de novo HF to its originating TD, including the infundibulum and all anagen HF lineages (Figures 1I and 2A, Figure 1—video 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of lineage tracing patterns.

claim: Continuous HF-to-TD-tracing pattern can only result from newly formed HFs originating from traced TD-epithelial cells.
source: As such a continuous HF-to-TD-tracing pattern can only result from newly formed HFs originating from traced TD-epithelial cells, we unequivocally demonstrated that these HFs were new.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the lineage tracing observations.

claim: De novo HF hair shafts were considerably shorter and thinner than hair shafts from both pre-existing HFs in the same mice and HFs in control mice with wild type phenotype.
source: An additional characteristic of de novo HFs was that their hair shafts were considerably shorter and thinner than hair shafts from both pre-existing HFs in the same mice (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl) and HFs in control mice with wild type phenotype (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements presented in the figure and source data.

claim: The HF-placode stage could be detected 10 days post tamoxifen administration in some TDs.
source: In some TDs, the HF-placode stage could be already detected 10 days post tamoxifen administration, and was accompanied by the appearance of a dermal condensate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The HF-placode stage was accompanied by the appearance of a dermal condensate.
source: In some TDs, the HF-placode stage could be already detected 10 days post tamoxifen administration, and was accompanied by the appearance of a dermal condensate (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The hair germ and hair peg stages were mostly detected between 27 and 29 days post tamoxifen administration.
source: The hair germ and hair peg stages were mostly detected between 27 and 29 days post tamoxifen administration (Figure 3B,C), and mature HFs, with a clearly visible developing hair shaft, emerged mainly at or after 33 days post tamoxifen administration (Figure 3D,D',F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Mature HFs, with a clearly visible developing hair shaft, emerged mainly at or after 33 days post tamoxifen administration.
source: The hair germ and hair peg stages were mostly detected between 27 and 29 days post tamoxifen administration (Figure 3B,C), and mature HFs, with a clearly visible developing hair shaft, emerged mainly at or after 33 days post tamoxifen administration (Figure 3D,D',F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Almost all dermal condensates and dermal papillae of de novo forming HFs were fully Tomato traced.
source: Interestingly, almost all dermal condensates and dermal papillae of de novo forming HFs were fully Tomato traced (Figure 3A–D,F), suggesting that either continuous high levels of Hh signaling in stromal cells (Ptch1fl/fl) are necessary for all stages of de novo HF development, or that stromal cells with constitutive Hh-pathway activation outcompete dermal condensate and dermal papilla cells with lower Hh-signaling levels.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Continuous high levels of Hh signaling in stromal cells (Ptch1fl/fl) may be necessary for all stages of de novo HF development.
source: Interestingly, almost all dermal condensates and dermal papillae of de novo forming HFs were fully Tomato traced (Figure 3A–D,F), suggesting that either continuous high levels of Hh signaling in stromal cells (Ptch1fl/fl) are necessary for all stages of de novo HF development, or that stromal cells with constitutive Hh-pathway activation outcompete dermal condensate and dermal papilla cells with lower Hh-signaling levels.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation.

claim: Stromal cells with constitutive Hh-pathway activation may outcompete dermal condensate and dermal papilla cells with lower Hh-signaling levels.
source: Interestingly, almost all dermal condensates and dermal papillae of de novo forming HFs were fully Tomato traced (Figure 3A–D,F), suggesting that either continuous high levels of Hh signaling in stromal cells (Ptch1fl/fl) are necessary for all stages of de novo HF development, or that stromal cells with constitutive Hh-pathway activation outcompete dermal condensate and dermal papilla cells with lower Hh-signaling levels.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation.

claim: Syndecan-1 (SDC1) expression marks early dermal condensates in wild type embryonic skin.
source: Importantly, Syndecan-1 (SDC1) expression that marks early dermal condensates in wild type embryonic skin (Figure 4A; Richardson et al., 2009), could already be detected 10 days post tamoxifen in dermal condensates of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin (Figure 4B), and was fully established in the dermal papilla at the hair germ stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and figure reference.

claim: SDC1 expression could be detected 10 days post tamoxifen in dermal condensates of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin.
source: Importantly, Syndecan-1 (SDC1) expression that marks early dermal condensates in wild type embryonic skin (Figure 4A; Richardson et al., 2009), could already be detected 10 days post tamoxifen in dermal condensates of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin (Figure 4B), and was fully established in the dermal papilla at the hair germ stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: SDC1 expression was fully established in the dermal papilla at the hair germ stage.
source: Importantly, Syndecan-1 (SDC1) expression that marks early dermal condensates in wild type embryonic skin (Figure 4A; Richardson et al., 2009), could already be detected 10 days post tamoxifen in dermal condensates of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin (Figure 4B), and was fully established in the dermal papilla at the hair germ stage (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The placodes (10 days post tamoxifen) as well as intermediate and mature developmental stages (5 weeks post tamoxifen) expressed Gli1 mRNA and have active Hh/Gli signaling.
source: The placodes (10 days post tamoxifen) as well as intermediate and mature developmental stages (5 weeks post tamoxifen) expressed Gli1 mRNA and hence have active Hh/Gli signaling (Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D); which is in line with normal embryonic HF development (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Chiang et al., 1999; St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from RNA-FISH.

claim: Active Hh/Gli signaling in de novo HFs is in line with normal embryonic HF development.
source: The placodes (10 days post tamoxifen) as well as intermediate and mature developmental stages (5 weeks post tamoxifen) expressed Gli1 mRNA and hence have active Hh/Gli signaling (Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D); which is in line with normal embryonic HF development (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A; Chiang et al., 1999; St-Jacques et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Wild type TD epithelial and stromal cells expressed Gli1 mRNA.
source: Wild type TD epithelial and stromal cells expressed Gli1 mRNA as expected (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Tomato-tracing (cells with Ptch1 deletion) and Gli1 expression were highly correlated.
source: This Gli1 RNA-FISH combined with antibody staining for Tomato-lineage tracing also confirmed that Tomato-tracing (cells with Ptch1 deletion) and Gli1 expression were highly correlated, as expected (Figure 4F–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HF formation in the Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mouse model is accompanied with BCC growth.
source: De novo HF formation in the Gli1creERT2; R26Tom; Ptch1fl/fl mouse model is accompanied with BCC growth; that is BCC-like lesions appear in pre-existing HF as well as in TDs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: BCC-like lesions in dorsal skin dramatically shrink within seven days upon vismodegib treatment.
source: It has been shown previously that BCC-like lesions in dorsal skin dramatically shrink within seven days upon vismodegib treatment (Eberl et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Vismodegib is a Hh-pathway inhibitor acting at the level of Smoothened (Smo).
source: Vismodegib is a Hh-pathway inhibitor acting at the level of Smoothened (Smo), and using the optimized treatment scheme from Eberl et al. (2018) we tested whether established de novo HFs would persist or would diminish as the BCC-tumor-growth area does.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vismodegib.

claim: In pre-existing HFs, vismodegib treatment resulted in considerable reduction of tumor size.
source: Reassuringly, in pre-existing HFs we found considerable reduction of tumor size (Figure 5B) as well as absence of Ki67 staining in Tomato-traced areas when comparing 7 day vismodegib treated samples with the untreated biopsies of the same mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Vismodegib treatment resulted in absence of Ki67 staining in Tomato-traced areas of pre-existing HFs.
source: Reassuringly, in pre-existing HFs we found considerable reduction of tumor size (Figure 5B) as well as absence of Ki67 staining in Tomato-traced areas when comparing 7 day vismodegib treated samples with the untreated biopsies of the same mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In TDs, the tumor areas dramatically diminished in size and Ki67 staining upon vismodegib treatment, however the de novo HFs persisted.
source: In TDs, the tumor areas also dramatically diminished in size and Ki67 staining, however the de novo HFs persisted (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HFs represent HFs that are independent of tumor structures as they persist upon vismodegib treatment when the surrounding BCC-tumor-growth areas are nearly gone.
source: In conclusion, these experiments confirmed that de novo HFs indeed represent HFs that are independent of tumor structures as they persist upon vismodegib treatment when the surrounding BCC-tumor-growth areas are nearly gone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vismodegib treatment experiments.

claim: BCC growth merely depends on epithelial Hh-pathway activation.
source: As BCC growth merely depends on epithelial Hh-pathway activation, it was tempting to test whether homozygous inactivation of Ptch1 exclusively in stromal cells would be sufficient to induce de novo HFs without tumor development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BCC.

claim: Administration of tamoxifen at 8 weeks of age in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice resulted in substantial Tomato-tracing that was restricted to the stromal skin compartment.
source: Administration of tamoxifen at 8 weeks of age resulted in substantial Tomato-tracing that was restricted to the stromal skin compartment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and importantly, the stromal cells of the TD were also traced (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The stromal cells of the TD were traced in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice.
source: Administration of tamoxifen at 8 weeks of age resulted in substantial Tomato-tracing that was restricted to the stromal skin compartment (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and importantly, the stromal cells of the TD were also traced (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Col1a2-expressing cells resulted in increased stromal cell density in TDs.
source: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Col1a2-expressing cells resulted in increased stromal cell density in TDs (Figure 6E), but did not result in de novo HF formation (Figure 6C,E), nor did stromal cells stain positive for SDC1 even 9 weeks after tamoxifen treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Col1a2-expressing cells did not result in de novo HF formation.
source: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Col1a2-expressing cells resulted in increased stromal cell density in TDs (Figure 6E), but did not result in de novo HF formation (Figure 6C,E), nor did stromal cells stain positive for SDC1 even 9 weeks after tamoxifen treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Stromal cells in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice did not stain positive for SDC1 even 9 weeks after tamoxifen treatment.
source: Homozygous Ptch1 inactivation in Col1a2-expressing cells resulted in increased stromal cell density in TDs (Figure 6E), but did not result in de novo HF formation (Figure 6C,E), nor did stromal cells stain positive for SDC1 even 9 weeks after tamoxifen treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Fully traced and highly condensed dermal clusters of cells (resembling dermal condensates) were detected in TD-adjacent infundibula and underneath the regular IFE in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice.
source: We also detected fully traced and highly condensed dermal clusters of cells (resembling dermal condensates) in TD-adjacent infundibula and underneath the regular IFE (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), which did not result in de novo HF induction and the dermal cell condensations were entirely negative for SDC1 expression (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Dermal cell condensations in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice did not result in de novo HF induction.
source: We also detected fully traced and highly condensed dermal clusters of cells (resembling dermal condensates) in TD-adjacent infundibula and underneath the regular IFE (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), which did not result in de novo HF induction and the dermal cell condensations were entirely negative for SDC1 expression (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Dermal cell condensations in Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice were entirely negative for SDC1 expression.
source: We also detected fully traced and highly condensed dermal clusters of cells (resembling dermal condensates) in TD-adjacent infundibula and underneath the regular IFE (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), which did not result in de novo HF induction and the dermal cell condensations were entirely negative for SDC1 expression (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Stromal activation of Hh signaling (Ptch1fl/fl) leads to increased stromal cell density and formation of cell condensates, however it is not sufficient to induce HF neogenesis in TDs nor elsewhere in skin without adjacent epithelial Hh-pathway activation.
source: We conclude that stromal activation of Hh signaling (Ptch1fl/fl) leads to increased stromal cell density and formation of cell condensates, however it is not sufficient to induce HF neogenesis in TDs nor elsewhere in skin without adjacent epithelial Hh-pathway activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Col1a2 mouse model experiments.

claim: Positive staining for both alkaline phosphatase (ALPL) and SDC1 expression was observed in the Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice at 10 days post tamoxifen.
source: Positive staining for both alkaline phosphatase (ALPL) and SDC1 expression was observed in the Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice, but not in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt, Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl, or Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Positive staining for both alkaline phosphatase (ALPL) and SDC1 expression was not observed in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt, Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl, or Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice at 10 days post tamoxifen.
source: Positive staining for both alkaline phosphatase (ALPL) and SDC1 expression was observed in the Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice, but not in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt, Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl, or Col1a2creER;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Only the Gli1 (Ptch1fl/fl) model bears TDs that are competent for de novo HF formation.
source: Altogether, staining for early signs of HF formation demonstrated that only the Gli1 (Ptch1fl/fl) model bears TDs that are competent for de novo HF formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of early markers across mouse models.

claim: The HF isthmus harbors adjacent epithelial and stromal Gli1-Tomato traced cells.
source: In addition to TDs, the HF isthmus also harbors adjacent epithelial and stromal Gli1-Tomato traced cells; the latter evident through Tomato/PDGFRb co-staining of stromal cells (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: At low frequency, de novo HFs were observed in the isthmus of pre-existing HFs in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin.
source: Thus, we re-examined the HF isthmus areas of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl skin for potential de novo HFs. Indeed, at low frequency, we observed de novo HFs in the isthmus of pre-existing HFs that were most likely newly formed (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HFs in the isthmus have not been observed in phenotypically normal control skin or in skin with HF tumors.
source: Such HFs have not been observed in phenotypically normal control skin (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt and Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/wt) or in skin with HF tumors (Lgr6creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl) (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: In the HF isthmus, Lgr6 expression is restricted to epithelial cells only, whereas Gli1 is expressed in epithelial and adjacent stromal cells.
source: Reassuringly, in the HF isthmus Lgr6 expression is restricted to epithelial cells only, whereas Gli1 is expressed in epithelial and adjacent stromal cells (Füllgrabe et al., 2015); suggesting that adjacent epithelial-stromal Hh signaling in areas outside of the TD may form de novo HFs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Adjacent epithelial-stromal Hh signaling in areas outside of the TD may form de novo HFs.
source: Reassuringly, in the HF isthmus Lgr6 expression is restricted to epithelial cells only, whereas Gli1 is expressed in epithelial and adjacent stromal cells (Füllgrabe et al., 2015); suggesting that adjacent epithelial-stromal Hh signaling in areas outside of the TD may form de novo HFs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the expression patterns and observations.

claim: The mouse hindpaw (plantar) epidermis is a skin region devoid of hair follicles and sweat glands.
source: The mouse hindpaw (plantar) epidermis is a skin region devoid of hair follicles and sweat glands, and is therefore ideal to test whether epithelial and stromal Hh-pathway activation can induce de novo HFs divorced from any confounding effects of nearby HF- or TD-niche signals (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mouse anatomy.

claim: Small Gli1-BGAL expressing clusters of epithelial and adjacent stromal cells were consistently found in the plantar skin.
source: When we probed for Gli1 expression in the plantar skin using Gli1LacZ reporter mice, we consistently found small Gli1-BGAL expressing clusters of epithelial and adjacent stromal cells in the plantar skin (Figure 9B, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A), which we confirmed with short-term lineage tracing in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom mice (tamoxifen at P8w; sample collection 7 days later) (Figure 9C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Numerous de novo HFs with hair shafts formed in the plantar skin of Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice.
source: Indeed, we found numerous de novo HFs with hair shafts in the normally hairless region. These HFs were fully Tomato-traced and showed normal inner-layer differentiation based on morphology and K6 staining (Figure 9D–E, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HFs in plantar skin were fully Tomato-traced and showed normal inner-layer differentiation based on morphology and K6 staining.
source: Indeed, we found numerous de novo HFs with hair shafts in the normally hairless region. These HFs were fully Tomato-traced and showed normal inner-layer differentiation based on morphology and K6 staining (Figure 9D–E, Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Combined epithelial and stromal Hh-pathway activation can induce de novo HFs independently of TD niches.
source: Taken together, the analysis of dorsal HF-isthmus as well as hairless paw skin demonstrated that combined epithelial and stromal Hh-pathway activation can induce de novo HFs independently of TD niches.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data from isthmus and paw skin.

claim: Hair follicle neogenesis in adult skin had only been observed under exceptional circumstances, such as upon repair of large wounds.
source: Hitherto, hair follicle neogenesis in adult skin had only been observed under exceptional circumstances, such as upon repair of large wounds (Breedis, 1954; Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: It is possible to induce HFs in small wounds upon supra-physiological Hh-pathway activation in the wound stroma.
source: A recent study found that it is possible to induce HFs even in small wounds upon supra-physiological Hh-pathway activation in the wound stroma (Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Modulation of Hh signaling is a new approach to induce de novo HFs in adult skin.
source: This report and our present study recognize modulation of Hh signaling as a new approach to induce de novo HFs in adult skin, and define activation in the stromal skin compartment as critical.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous research.

claim: Activation in the stromal skin compartment is critical for inducing de novo HFs.
source: This report and our present study recognize modulation of Hh signaling as a new approach to induce de novo HFs in adult skin, and define activation in the stromal skin compartment as critical.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and previous research.

claim: Wounding of skin initiates a major reorganization of the epithelial and mesenchymal tissue including the activation and differentiation of a large number of cell types.
source: As wounding of skin initiates a major reorganization of the epithelial and mesenchymal tissue including the activation and differentiation of a large number of cell types (Arwert et al., 2012; Joost et al., 2018; Schäfer and Werner, 2008), and may even provide an embryonic-like environment (Wang et al., 2015), the precise (e.g. minimal) molecular signals that are required for HF induction in adult skin remain elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Wounding may provide an embryonic-like environment.
source: As wounding of skin initiates a major reorganization of the epithelial and mesenchymal tissue including the activation and differentiation of a large number of cell types (Arwert et al., 2012; Joost et al., 2018; Schäfer and Werner, 2008), and may even provide an embryonic-like environment (Wang et al., 2015), the precise (e.g. minimal) molecular signals that are required for HF induction in adult skin remain elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The precise (e.g. minimal) molecular signals that are required for HF induction in adult skin remain elusive.
source: As wounding of skin initiates a major reorganization of the epithelial and mesenchymal tissue including the activation and differentiation of a large number of cell types (Arwert et al., 2012; Joost et al., 2018; Schäfer and Werner, 2008), and may even provide an embryonic-like environment (Wang et al., 2015), the precise (e.g. minimal) molecular signals that are required for HF induction in adult skin remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: In unwounded skin, experimentally elevated Hh signaling in epithelial and adjacent stromal cells was sufficient to induce de novo HFs.
source: Here we revealed that in unwounded skin, experimentally elevated Hh signaling in epithelial and adjacent stromal cells was sufficient to induce de novo HFs, extending our understanding of how Hh signaling can be modulated to induce HFs in adult skin.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: To achieve efficient de novo HF induction in unwounded skin, supra-physiological Hh signaling in both compartments, the epithelium and stroma, was necessary.
source: To achieve efficient de novo HF induction in unwounded skin, supra-physiological Hh signaling in both compartments, the epithelium and stroma, was necessary.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing different mouse models.

claim: Normal TD maintenance requires active and balanced Hh signaling in adjacent epithelial and stromal cells.
source: Normal TD maintenance also requires active and balanced Hh signaling in adjacent epithelial and stromal cells (Figure 4E; Xiao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and figure reference.

claim: Increased Hh-signaling levels in TD epithelial cells result in BCC-like tumors, even though stromal cells have active (albeit physiological) Hh signaling.
source: Increased Hh-signaling levels in TD epithelial cells result in BCC-like tumors, even though stromal cells have active (albeit physiological) Hh signaling.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: To effectively induce de novo HFs in TDs, high levels of Hh/Gli signaling in both compartments were necessary.
source: Importantly therefore, to effectively induce de novo HFs in TDs, high levels of Hh/Gli signaling in both compartments were necessary (Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: β-catenin-induced de novo HF formation was not only dependent on stromal Hh signaling, but also required two intact Smo alleles (for a maximal Hh-pathway activation) to enable efficient de novo HF induction.
source: This requirement of Hh-signal activation at precise levels and in the right compartments is in agreement with a recent study demonstrating that β-catenin-induced de novo HF formation was not only dependent on stromal Hh signaling, but also required two intact Smo alleles (for a maximal Hh-pathway activation) to enable efficient de novo HF induction (Lichtenberger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Activation of epithelial β-catenin in mouse skin can induce new HFs.
source: It has been shown more than twenty years ago that the activation of epithelial β-catenin in mouse skin can induce new HFs (Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004), and more recently that activation of epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases de novo HF formation within wounds (Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Activation of epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases de novo HF formation within wounds.
source: It has been shown more than twenty years ago that the activation of epithelial β-catenin in mouse skin can induce new HFs (Gat et al., 1998; Lo Celso et al., 2004), and more recently that activation of epithelial Wnt/β-catenin signaling increases de novo HF formation within wounds (Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Wnt signaling has to be blocked in dermal fibroblasts to allow de novo HF induction during wound regeneration.
source: However, Wnt signaling has to be blocked in dermal fibroblasts to allow de novo HF induction during wound regeneration (Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Early stage BCCs resemble early stages of HF development and both are dependent on Wnt- and Hh-pathway activation.
source: It is known that early stage BCCs resemble early stages of HF development and both are dependent on Wnt- and Hh-pathway activation, with the major morphological difference that BCC lacks a dermal condensate (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The major morphological difference between early stage BCCs and early stages of HF development is that BCC lacks a dermal condensate.
source: It is known that early stage BCCs resemble early stages of HF development and both are dependent on Wnt- and Hh-pathway activation, with the major morphological difference that BCC lacks a dermal condensate (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: By coordinating the activation of Hh/Gli signaling (cell type specific and high levels), de novo HFs were induced by 'redirecting' some of the BCC buds to HF formation without the need of wounding.
source: Indeed, by coordinating the activation of Hh/Gli signaling (cell type specific and high levels) we were able to induce de novo HFs by 'redirecting' some of the BCC buds to HF formation without the need of wounding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HF induction occurred in the presence of oncogenic signal activation (i.e. presence of a tumor environment or tumor-like cellular status of Ptch1fl/fl HF-inducing epithelial cells).
source: Nevertheless, this induction occurred in the presence of oncogenic signal activation (i.e. presence of a tumor environment or tumor-like cellular status of Ptch1fl/fl HF-inducing epithelial cells) which may to some extent mimic a wounding situation (Dvorak, 1986).
evidence: This is an observation and interpretation of the experimental conditions.

claim: Oncogenic signal activation may to some extent mimic a wounding situation.
source: Nevertheless, this induction occurred in the presence of oncogenic signal activation (i.e. presence of a tumor environment or tumor-like cellular status of Ptch1fl/fl HF-inducing epithelial cells) which may to some extent mimic a wounding situation (Dvorak, 1986).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: Whenever de novo HFs were to be found, either oncogenic signaling or a wound environment was involved.
source: The molecular and cellular similarities of tumorigenesis and wound healing are still unfolding, yet whenever de novo HFs were to be found, either oncogenic signaling or a wound environment was involved.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the field.

claim: In order to overcome inhibitory signals, de novo HF morphogenesis in adult skin may require major activating signals provided by oncogenesis or wounding.
source: This supports the long-standing recognition of the similarity between tumor and wound healing signaling (tumors as 'wounds that do not heal') – and raises the key question of what exactly is the relationship between tumorigenesis and signals inducing de novo HF formation? It may indeed be the case that in order to overcome inhibitory signals, de novo HF morphogenesis in adult skin requires such major activating signals provided by oncogenesis or wounding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Only initial HF placode and/or dermal condensate formation may require strong signals whereas progression to a mature HF does not require continued tumorigenic or wound signaling.
source: Interestingly however, previous literature suggests that only initial HF placode and/or dermal condensate formation may require such strong signals whereas progression to a mature HF does not require continued tumorigenic or wound signaling (Brown et al., 2017; Ito et al., 2007; Lo Celso et al., 2004; Silva-Vargas et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HF tumors require continuous Wnt/β-catenin signaling, whereas transient activation of this pathway is sufficient to induce de novo HFs in adult mouse epidermis.
source: For example, HF tumors require continuous Wnt/β-catenin signaling, whereas transient activation of this pathway is sufficient to induce de novo HFs in adult mouse epidermis (Lo Celso et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Non-mutant cells, remaining from regressed Wnt/β-catenin induced tumor outgrowths, could develop into new functional HFs.
source: More recently, intra vital imaging from Wnt/β-catenin induced tumor outgrowths demonstrated that non-mutant cells, remaining from regressed outgrowths, could develop into new functional HFs.
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous research.

claim: Tumor outgrowth depended on the presence of mutated cells, however the new appendages were formed from wild type cells facilitated by their (altered) niche environment.
source: Most interestingly, tumor outgrowth depended on the presence of mutated cells, however the new appendages were formed from wild type cells facilitated by their (altered) niche environment (Brown et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: De novo HF induction without accompanied tumor growth in unwounded adult skin may in principle be possible, if the right signals at the right time and restricted period, and in the right compartments were provided.
source: Taken together, these are promising examples that de novo HF induction without accompanied tumor growth in unwounded adult skin may in principle be possible, if the right signals at the right time and restricted period, and in the right compartments were provided.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the literature and current findings.

claim: Nearly all de novo HFs in plantar skin developed without attendant BCC-like lesions.
source: Strikingly, we observed numerous de novo HFs throughout this nominally hairless skin in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice. Crucially, nearly all these de novo HFs developed without attendant BCC-like lesions suggesting that de novo HF morphogenesis may indeed be successfully initiated without a tumor microenvironment; while the vismodegib experiment suggests persistence of such structures when the tumor microenvironment regresses in dorsal skin.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: De novo HF morphogenesis may be successfully initiated without a tumor microenvironment.
source: Strikingly, we observed numerous de novo HFs throughout this nominally hairless skin in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice. Crucially, nearly all these de novo HFs developed without attendant BCC-like lesions suggesting that de novo HF morphogenesis may indeed be successfully initiated without a tumor microenvironment; while the vismodegib experiment suggests persistence of such structures when the tumor microenvironment regresses in dorsal skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paw skin observations.

claim: The vismodegib experiment suggests persistence of de novo HFs when the tumor microenvironment regresses in dorsal skin.
source: Strikingly, we observed numerous de novo HFs throughout this nominally hairless skin in Gli1creERT2;R26Tom;Ptch1fl/fl mice. Crucially, nearly all these de novo HFs developed without attendant BCC-like lesions suggesting that de novo HF morphogenesis may indeed be successfully initiated without a tumor microenvironment; while the vismodegib experiment suggests persistence of such structures when the tumor microenvironment regresses in dorsal skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the vismodegib treatment experiments.

claim: Molecular strategies for the induction of complex epithelial structures in the adult remain a major challenge in regenerative medicine.
source: In sum, molecular strategies for the induction of complex epithelial structures in the adult remain a major challenge in regenerative medicine.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Cell-type specific modulation of a single pathway was sufficient to induce complex epithelial structures in the adult body.
source: Our study demonstrates that cell-type specific modulation of a single pathway was sufficient to induce complex epithelial structures in the adult body, a discovery aiding our understanding of adult tissue biology and regenerative medicine.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by experimental data.
